doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: US Expat and Digital Nomad Taxes
text:
The United States is one of only two countries that taxes citizens on worldwide income regardless of where they live.

While this means Americans abroad must continue filing taxes, several provisions can significantly reduce or eliminate your tax burden when living abroad.

Table of Contents

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: The Reality of the Situation
text:
Unlike nearly every other country, the U.S. taxes based on citizenship, not residency. This means:

  - You must file U.S. tax returns even if you haven't set foot in America all year
  - All worldwide income is potentially taxable
  - This applies whether you're a permanent expat or digital nomad
  - The only way to stop filing is to renounce citizenship (a serious decision with its own tax implications)

However, the tax code provides substantial relief for expats through exclusions, deductions, and credits that can reduce your U.S. tax bill to zero—if you qualify and plan properly.

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Foreign Earned Income Exclusion
text:
The FEIE allows you to exclude up to $130,000 (2025) of foreign earned income from U.S. taxation. For married couples filing jointly, each spouse can claim the exclusion if both have foreign earned income.

What Qualifies as "Earned Income":

Included:

  - Salaries and wages
  - Self-employment income
  - Professional fees
  - Commissions and bonuses

Not Included:

  - Investment income
  - Capital gains
  - Rental income
  - Pension distributions

Two Ways to Qualify:

1. Physical Presence Test

  - Be outside the U.S. for 330 full days in any 12-month period
  - Days don't need to be consecutive
  - Partial days in the U.S. count as U.S. days
  - Most straightforward qualification method

2. Bona Fide Residence Test

  - Be a bona fide resident of a foreign country for an entire tax year
  - Requires establishing genuine ties (home, bank accounts, local tax filing)
  - More flexible for U.S. visits
  - More complex to prove

Important Limitations:

  - This is an exclusion, not a deduction—it doesn't lower your tax bracket for remaining income
  - Cannot be used to offset investment income or capital gains
  - Self-employment tax still applies (15.3% on net earnings)
  - Must file Form 2555 to claim

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Foreign Housing Exclusion/Deduction
text:
In addition to the FEIE, you can exclude or deduct qualifying foreign housing expenses that exceed a base amount.

How It Works:

Base Amount: 16% of FEIE maximum (20,240for2025) **MaximumExclusion:**Generally30%ofFEIE(37,950 for 2025) Your Benefit: Actual housing costs minus base amount

Qualifying Expenses:

Included:

  - Rent
  - Utilities (except phone)
  - Property insurance
  - Parking at residence
  - Furniture rental

Not Included:

  - Mortgage payments
  - Purchased furniture
  - Domestic labor
  - TV/Internet subscriptions

High-Cost Cities Exception:

Certain cities have higher limits recognizing their extreme housing costs:

  - Hong Kong, London, Tokyo: Higher caps apply
  - IRS publishes annual list of adjusted limits
  - Can exclude substantially more in these locations

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Foreign Tax Credit (FTC)
text:
The FTC provides a dollar-for-dollar credit for foreign income taxes paid, potentially more valuable than the FEIE for high earners in high-tax countries.

Key Advantages:

  - No income limit (unlike FEIE)
  - Unused credits carry back 1 year or forward 10 years
  - Can be used on investment income
  - May result in larger refund than FEIE

Strategic Considerations:

Choose FTC over FEIE when:

  - Living in a high-tax country (most of Europe)
  - Significant investment income
  - Income exceeds FEIE limits
  - Want to maintain U.S. retirement account eligibility

Combine both when possible:

  - Use FEIE on earned income
  - Use FTC on investment income
  - Cannot double-dip on same income

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Self-Employment Tax Strategies
text:
Self-employed expats face a particular challenge: FEIE doesn't reduce self-employment tax (15.3% on net earnings up to $160,200 in 2025).

Mitigation Strategies:

S-Corporation Election

  - Pay yourself reasonable salary (subject to payroll tax)
  - Take remaining profit as distributions (not subject to SE tax)
  - Requires additional compliance but can save thousands

Solo 401(k)

  - Contribute up to $23,500 as employee
  - Additional ~20% of net SE income as employer
  - Reduces taxable income significantly

Totalization Agreements

  - U.S. has agreements with 30+ countries
  - Avoid double social security taxation
  - Pay into only one system
  - Check if your country has an agreement

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: State Tax Complications
text:
Your last state of residence may still try to tax you. Some states are particularly aggressive.

Sticky States:

Most Aggressive:

  - California: Presumes continued residency unless proven otherwise
  - New York: Scrutinizes ties and days present
  - Virginia: Difficult domicile rules

Most Favorable:

  - No state tax: Alaska, Florida, Nevada, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington, Wyoming
  - Easy to establish and break residency

Breaking State Ties:

Before leaving:

  - Change driver's license
  - Register to vote elsewhere
  - Close local bank accounts
  - Sell or rent primary residence
  - Document your departure

Consider intermediate move:

  - Establish residency in no-tax state before going abroad
  - Spend sufficient time to establish domicile
  - Provides clean break from high-tax state

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Reporting Requirements
text:
Beyond regular tax returns, expats face additional reporting obligations with severe penalties for non-compliance.

FBAR (FinCEN Form 114):

  - Required if foreign accounts exceed $10,000 aggregate at any point
  - Due April 15 (automatic extension to October 15)
  - Penalties: Up to $250,000 and 5 years imprisonment for willful violations

Form 8938 (FATCA):

  - Required if foreign assets exceed thresholds ($200,000 single, $400,000 married)
  - Filed with tax return
  - Penalties start at $10,000

Form 5471 (Foreign Corporation):

  - Required if you own 10%+ of foreign corporation
  - Extremely complex reporting
  - Penalty: $10,000+ per form per year

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Practical Planning Strategies
text:
Timing Your Move:

Best times to become an expat:

  - January: Full year for bona fide residence test
  - After receiving large bonus/commission
  - Before exercising stock options
  - When investment income is low

Income Optimization:

Accelerate before leaving:

  - Bonuses and commissions
  - Stock option exercises
  - Business sale

Defer until abroad:

  - Consulting income
  - Freelance work
  - New employment

Investment Considerations:

Problems to avoid:

  - Foreign mutual funds (PFIC rules = tax nightmare)
  - Foreign tax-deferred accounts (often taxable in U.S.)
  - U.S. state municipal bonds (may lose tax exemption)

Better alternatives:

  - U.S.-based index funds
  - Direct real estate investment
  - Individual stocks

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Common Pitfalls
text:
✗ Assuming no U.S. tax obligations - You must file regardless of foreign tax paid

✗ Missing the FEIE election deadline - Generally must be claimed by original due date plus extensions

✗ Maintaining unnecessary state ties - Can result in continued state tax liability

✗ DIY approach for complex situations - Professional help often pays for itself

✗ Ignoring reporting requirements - Penalties can exceed tax savings

✗ Poor documentation - Keep detailed records of days present, foreign taxes, housing costs

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Key Takeaways
text:
✓ U.S. citizens must file taxes worldwide but multiple provisions can eliminate most or all U.S. tax

✓ The FEIE can exclude $126,500 of earned income if you meet physical presence or residency tests

Peter Thiel, Mitt Romney, and Ted Wescler all built $100M+ Roth IRAs. The funny thing is that these strategies are available to everyone!

[In this post], I’m going to take you behind the scenes of four separate individuals that have grown their Roth IRA to extremely large amounts — from hundreds of millions to billions of dollars.

A Roth IRA was never intended by the IRS to get so big.

But since there is no legislation prohibiting it, some of the most sophisticated investors have used the tax code to massively grow these accounts to bypass tens or hundreds of millions of dollars in taxes.

Using fully legal strategies available to you.

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: The Peter Thiel $5B Roth IRA
text:
Peter Thiel may own the[ most famous Roth IRA of all time].

It started in 1999 — he was starting Paypal, and under the $110,000 Roth IRA income limit and was able to contribute $2,000 to get his account started.

However, instead of investing it in stocks or ETF’s, he used it to buy his founder shares in Paypal — spending $1,700 to buy 1.7 million shares at $0.001/share.

How was he able to do this?

Before a startup raises outside financing, a brand new company is typically deemed to have a par value of almost nothing… typically a few hundred or few thousand dollars.

Founders can buy their shares at incredibly low values, and when the company raises external financing, the internal or 409a share price goes up.

After that initial contribution, Thiel never had to contribute a single other dollar to his Roth IRA.

When Paypal sold to eBay in 2002, Thiel made $28.5M on the sale — and since the dollars were inside his Roth IRA, he owed zero taxes.

But more importantly, he was now relatively young with tens of millions of dollars in his Roth IRA!

This account then became supercharged tax-free investment vehicle.

From that point on, he used his Roth IRA to invest in all kinds of assets, including founder shares in Palantir (now worth $100B+) and the seed round of Meta (now worth $1T+).

His Roth IRA is now conservatively worth at least $5B and likely substantially more.

And he gets access to all of it with zero taxes in less than 2 years!

Should we try and emulate Thiel?

The IRS has very clear rules limiting “self-dealing” inside retirement accounts.

This effectively means a transaction inside a Roth IRA cannot be deemed to be benefitting you as an individual in any way. As an example, you cannot invest in a house and then also live in it.

If you are caught “self-dealing”, your entire Roth IRA could be rendered invalid so it’s super high risk and worth steering clear of.

While Thiel likely got very good legal advice approving the transaction, my personal understanding is it’s substantially safer to avoid buying shares in a private company where you are also the founder.

There is likely a[ fair bit of nuance] based on exactly how much of the company you own, and Thiel may have been under the limit, but you could potentially be playing with fire.

However, you can likely achieve similar outcomes by buying private startup shares as an early employee, advisor or investor while taking a lot less risk of blowing yourself up.

title: The Ted Weschler $250M Roth IRA
text:
Ted Weschler, the investment manager at Berkshire Hathaway started saving for retirement all the way back in 1984.

He started contributing to his 401k plan at work so that he could get the full match from his employer.

Eventually, he transferred those assets into a self-directed IRA so that he could decide exactly which stocks to invest in.

title: How doable is this for a regular rich person?

  - You start making contributions to a Roth IRA by age 19, and start maxing it out by age 23.
  - You started making 401k contributions using the mega backdoor loophole by age 23 and max it out by age 30.
  - The maximum contribution limits stay where they are today and I plugged in the 100-year average return for the S&P 500 including dividends.

Simplified model to see what a regular rich person Roth IRA could get to

Powerful stuff.

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Understanding and Negotiating Your Startup Equity
text:
Most people who work at a startup have no idea how much their equity is worth!

I wrote this guide to help startup employees understand the value of their equity and negotiate to get more value.

Table of Contents

-----

[One of the best parts] of working at a startup is you typically have the opportunity to own a piece of the business.

If the startup ends up being massively successful, you directly participate in the upside as a small owner.

However, almost every startup employee has absolutely no idea how to actually value their equity.

The information employees do receive about their equity reads like complete jargon.

Founders sometimes intentionally withhold important data that anyone joining the company should know.

And, employees remain in the dark about a huge part of their compensation since they don’t even know what questions to ask!

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: How to Think About Equity
text:
Equity is ownership of a piece of a company.

When you buy shares of a company in the stock market, you own equity in the public company. When a startup gives you shares or stock options, you own equity in the startup.

Almost every wealthy person made their money by owning equities that substantially increased in value.

You also typically pay a much lower tax rate when you sell equity versus the salary you earn.

As a startup employee, here are some of the important considerations as you think about the equity part of your compensation.

  - Business Quality

The single most important factor in valuing your startup equity is the quality of the underlying startup.

A tiny piece of a phenomenal business is worth infinitely more than a large piece of a company that goes to zero.

When startups get massively big (think Uber or OpenAI or SpaceX), almost every single equity holder ends up making a lot of money.

  - Equity does not pay the bills

While equity presents one of the best opportunities for asymmetric upside, you cannot pay your bills with equity.

Startup equity is a highly speculative asset.

Even if you own many millions of dollars of stock options in a startup, it’s prudent to think of it as paper money until you see actual liquidity. This means you should not spend real money based on your paper net worth.

  - Think like an investor

As a startup employee, you are not that effectively a startup investor with one major caveat:

You can only “invest” your time in one startup at a time.

Investors can afford to take a portfolio of bets, while you get only one bet at a time — and a handful of bets over your entire career.

Working for a company that you think has a really high probability of being worth a lot of money someday is a solid approach to equity.

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: How to Value your Equity (part 1)
text:
Most employees of early stage startups receive stock options.

For the next two sections, I’ll be assuming you own stock options, though restricted shares work very similarly with slightly better tax benefits.

Understanding Startup Math:

The most important equation to learn is:

Company value = Number of shares in the company * Share price

If you ever know two of the three numbers above, you can calculate the third with simple arithmetic. This equation works for tiny startups, and large public companies alike.

The tricky thing is early-stage startups typically have two distinct prices at any given time. These are:

The “Internal” Price or 409a Price

This is the share price at which the company grants you equity.

When you receive stock options, you will see reference to a “strike price” — this is what you would have to pay to exercise or buy your stock options.

Companies need to hire third-party auditors once a year to calculate this internal share price.

Since this is the price employees have to pay out of pocket to buy their shares, companies typically want to drive this price as low as possible.

The “External” Price or Preferred Price

This is the share price at which the company raises money.

Companies want this price to be as high as possible since the cost of the capital becomes cheaper the greater the valuation.

Technically, investors receive a different class of shares for this higher price called preferred shares. These shares have a couple of important benefits I’ll talk about later.

-----

Calculating The Value of Your Equity:

You can use the difference between these two prices to calculate the present value of your equity today:

Value of your equity = Number of shares you own * (External Price - Internal Price)

In order to calculate the value of your equity, you need to ask your employer for the share price at which the most recent funding round was conducted.

If the startup has not raised a priced round yet, they may not have an official preferred share price. But, you can use the valuation of the last SAFE note to approximate what this can be.

There are a few other important factors to consider when valuing your equity:

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: How to Value your Equity (part 2)
text:
1.  How long you have to stick around to earn this equity  
      
     Most equity has to be earned out over a period of time - this is referred to as “vesting” your equity.  
      
     You can take the total time period over which your equity vests to calculate exactly how much you are earn in equity every single year:  
      
     Annual value of your equity = Value of your equity / Total years of vesting required  
      
     Pay attention to the “cliff” in your vesting schedule — this is the minimum amount of time you have to stick around to receive anything at all.  
      
2.  Every time the company raises at a higher valuation, the value of your equity goes up  
      
     When the company raises a new round of financing, the preferred share price moves to a new higher price.  
      
     This can substantially increase your equity compensation without you receiving more shares.  
      
     If you join a startup when it’s tiny, and it grows to be worth billions of dollars, this can end up being a dramatic amount of equity.  
      
3.  Companies raising at a lower valuation can be catastrophically bad  
      
     If your startup has a “down round” and has to raise money at a lower valuation, this can sometimes wipe out the entire value of your equity.  
      
     While it rarely happens, if the startup ever raises money at a share price lower than your strike price, your options are entirely worthless or “underwater” and you need to talk to your founders about it ASAP.  
      

Startup Equity Calculator

I spent 30 minutes playing around to build a very useful[ Startup Equity calculator]. You can use this tool to plug in your numbers and see exactly how much your equity is worth.

You can input your vesting schedule and see exactly how much you end up vesting every year.

It also supports scenario modeling at different exit prices, so you can see what youe equity could be worth in the future too!

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Other Considerations in Evaluating Equity (part 1)
text:
Beyond calculating the dollar value of your equity, there are a few other considerations to be aware of.

All of these can dramatically affect the final outcome in how much your equity actually ends up mattering.

Percentage Ownership:

Every employee has the right to know what percentage of the startup they own.

In order to calculate this, you need to know how many total shares exist at any given time. This is the equation:

Percentage ownership = Your shares / Total number of shares in the company

If you find that your company or founder is reluctant to share this information, I’d consider this a major red flag.

Two important notes on percentage ownership:

  - Use it to benchmark your compensation  
      
     Ownership percentage is the best way to benchmark if you are being compensated fairly, particularly for senior roles.  
      
     You can typically find data on how much equity people at similar-sized companies with the same title are receiving.  
      
  - Your ownership will change with time  
      
     Your percentage ownership will keep changing with time as the company raises more money.  
      
     Every time the company fundraises, the total number of shares increase.  
      
     This means you will get “diluted” as your shares now represent a smaller percentage of the business. This is totally fine as long as the dollar value of your equity keeps growing.  
      

Liquidation Preference:

When investors invest in a startup, they typically receive *preferred* shares that have slightly different rights over common shares that employees receive.

The most important right they typically get is a *liquidation preference*. This allows them to receive their initial investment back before ANY common shareholder (including you) ever get paid out.

The upshot of this is the company needs to sell for AT LEAST the total liquidation preference before any common shareholder receives any money.

How do you calculate the liquidation preference?

This is usually the total amount of capital the startup has ever raised.

But, you should always ask for confirmation as sometimes companies owe a multiple on the dollars raised, which can make seeing a return quite challenging!

Typically, the liquidation preference does not matter much when a company has a successful exit.

But if you are evaluating working for a company that has raised hundreds of millions of dollars, it’s certainly worth factoring in.

Post-Termination Exercise Period (PTEP)

Choosing to exercise your stock options can be quite expensive.

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Other Considerations in Evaluating Equity (part 2)
text:
To convert your options into actual shares, you need to buy them for the strike price multiplied by the total number of shares. Based on how much equity you have, this can cost tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars!

This is also a very risky investment as startup equity is a highly speculative asset. If the company fails, you end up with nothing.

Most people tend to wait until an exit is around the corner and only exercise their options when they are guaranteed to make money.

If you still work at the company, this is a great strategy.

However, if you don’t still work at the company, most companies have a clause that give you only a fixed number of days after terminating employment to come up with the cash to exercise your stock options!

This amount of time is called the *Post-Termination Exercise Period* (PTEP).

Historically, companies had a PTEP of only 90 days. This meant if you quit your job, you had to scramble for the cash in 3 months if you wanted to keep your equity.

Thankfully, most modern startups are electing for much longer PTEP windows. This is definitely something you should ask about if your stock options cost a meaningful amount of money to exercise.

At my startup Carry, we give everyone 10 years after employment to exercise their stock options.

Company Financial Health:

Startups succeed for lots of different reasons, but every startup fails because they run out of cash.

As you are evaluating startup equity, ensure you ask the founders for a snapshot of the company’s overall health.

Some things I would ask about:

  - How much cash the company currently has in the bank
  - How much cash the company is burning every month (net of revenue) - you can use this to infer how many months of “runway” they have
  - Company revenue numbers and growth rates

If you have friends that are VC investors, it can be very helpful to get their perspective on how they would value a company with these specific metrics.

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: How to Negotiate Your Equity (part 1)
text:
Let’s bring this entire article together.

Here’s a step-by-step guide on how you should negotiate equity before accepting a job offer.

Step 1: Find a startup you believe in

This is the single most important step in the process.

Great companies are rare, and you’d rather own a small piece of a phenomenal company than a big piece of anything else.

One strategy for finding great companies can be asking prolific investors what startups in their portfolio they are most excited about.

Step 2: Ask for the information you need to calculate the value of your equity

At the job offer stage, ensure the company shares the following information with you:

  - How many total shares are outstanding
  - Your percentage ownership (you can use the total shares to calculate this)
  - The most recent fundraising valuation and preferred share price
  - The vesting schedule

Plug those numbers into the[ Startup Equity Calculator] and see what your equity could look like at different exit scenarios.

Also, ask about the liquidation preference, company health and the post-termination exercise window to look for any potential red flags.

Step 3: Pull equity benchmarks and see how you stack up

This is more relevant for senior roles, but look for equity benchmarks for your specific role by company size and location.

If you don’t have access to compensation data, ask the hiring manager or founder to share their data and how they derived the equity grant.

You can also find equity benchmarks by how early a hire you are at a startup:

Step 4: Negotiate for what’s important to you

There are many different levers for negotiating equity — but I’d focus on what is specifically important to you.

If you are more excited about equity and don’t need a lot of cash to support your current lifestyle, most startup job offers will let you trade some of your cash compensation for more equity.

Don’t forget that equity doesn’t pay the bills!

If a company is refusing to budge on the quantity of equity, it may be worth seeing if you can push on some of the other terms like the vesting time period or post-termination exercise period.

Step 5: Revisit this annually

While companies typically do not offer refresher grants every year, it’s worth keeping track of how much equity you are vesting annually.

If the company raises money at a much higher valuation, the value of your equity could noticeably appreciate.

If your role has a bonus component, you could ask your startup if they would consider granting part of the bonus in equity.

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: How to Negotiate Your Equity (part 2)
text:
If you ever receive a significant promotion, you should push to see if you can also receive more equity as part of that move.

Ultimately, the best way of owning more equity is to do a phenomenal job. Companies like to generously reward top performers with a meaningful amount of equity.

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: The Self-Employed Tax Saving Handbook
text:
Self-employed entrepreneurs have the most tax strategies at their disposal. But most of them never take advantage of them (simply because they don’t know about them!)

-----

[I came across a fascinating post] on Twitter recently.

A solo business owner who makes over a million dollars a year broke down exactly what he spends money on.

What is the first thing you notice?

He’s paying more than $400,000 in taxes every single year!

I don’t know Brett personally but I know lots of Brett’s — incredibly successful independent business owners facing absolutely monstrous tax bills.

Between self-employment taxes, state taxes and federal taxes, without smart planning, I’ve seen effective tax rates of over 50% in states like New York and California.

This article is a guide on exactly what you should do in his situation to dramatically reduce your tax bill.

Results will vary by your personal situation, but if you are fully unoptimized, this guide should enable you to knock off at least 6 figures a year at those numbers.

While there are literally hundreds of strategies for business owners to save money on taxes, I’m going to focus on the five most impactful ones here.

I’ll end with a section for miscellaneous tips and strategies where I’ll share a longer list of ideas that may be less impactful, but could still add up.

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Strategy 1: Elect to file your taxes as an S-Corp (part 1)
text:
The first nasty surprise you typically discover as a business owner is employment taxes.

When you have a full-time job, you typically only pay half of social security and medicare taxes, while your employer pays the other half. It’s also automatically deducted from your paycheck so you don’t feel the pain quite as viscerally.

But when you work for yourself, you are on the hook for both sides of employment taxes, which could be as much as 15% of every single paycheck!

This 15% is in addition to regular federal and state income taxes you owe… which in higher brackets can easily take your overall tax rate over 50%.

Filing your taxes as an S-Corporation is the best way of bringing this number down.

Here’s how an S-Corp works:

An S-Corp bifurcates your business income into two distinct components:

  - W-2 salary: A fair market salary that you pay yourself as an employee of the S-Corp. This should be a salary that you would reasonably pay someone else to do the same job as an employee for your business.
  - Profit distributions: The remaining income flows to you as profit as the business owner.

The magic of an S-Corp is you only pay employment taxes on the W-2 salary, so this can potentially save you tens of thousands of dollars in taxes.

From the original example, without an S-Corp, Brett would have to pay employment taxes on the entire $1M. But if he chose to pay himself a W-2 salary of 200,000,hewouldnothavetopayanyemploymenttaxesontheremaining~800,000!

While most high income business owners are generally better off filing taxes as an S-Corp, there are some important caveats to consider:

1 - Complexity

An S-Corp does take more effort to run since you now need payroll and a separate tax return. I tend to think at $100K+ in net income it’s fully worth the additional hassle, but lots of other professionals advertise a lower number.

Personally, I would want to save at least a few thousand dollars to make the additional work worth my time.

2 - Have a tax pro run the numbers

I would not DIY an S-Corp analysis, since there are a bunch of weird edge cases that a qualified tax professional can correctly identify.

As an example, an S-Corp in New York City faces an additional business tax that a pass-through LLC would not. For residents in NYC specifically, the threshold at which an S-Corp is worth it becomes much higher than typical.

3 - Picking the right W-2 salary is important

You may be tempted to pick the lowest W-2 salary you can since that would result in the lowest employment taxes.

But, this can sometimes have the adverse effect of increasing your overall taxes since it could reduce your QBI deduction! Your retirement plan contributions are also based on the W-2 you pay yourself.

We’ll talk more about this soon.

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Strategy 2: Hire your spouse and double your Solo 401k contribution
text:
A[ Solo 401k] if you are eligible for it.

A quick recap: with a Solo 401k you can get up to a $70,000 tax deduction, invest in any almost asset class, compound tax-free, make Roth contributions and get a tax credit for setting one up.

The only thing better than a Solo 401k as a business owner?

Two Solo 401k’s.

The easiest way for a successful business owner to “double down” on this benefit is to hire their spouse for their business.

Assuming you pay your spouse a reasonable enough salary, this would now allow them to also get their own $70,000 Solo 401k tax deduction — and you can collectively as a couple now deduct $140,000 from your taxes every single year

If you are over the age of 50, that’s an extra $7,500 each or a $155,000 tax deduction between the both of you.

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Strategy 3: Add a cash balance plan for an even bigger retirement contribution
text:
For the truly high income business owners, there is a special type of retirement plan available with an even bigger tax deduction.

It’s called a[ Cash Balance Plans] and can potentially get you an annual tax deduction of hundreds of thousands of dollars and pairs very well with a Solo 401k.

A cash balance plan is a type of “defined benefit” retirement plan that works backwards from giving you $3.5 million at retirement age.

The maximum pre-tax contribution you can make is a somewhat complicated actuarial formula calculated based on:

  - Your age
  - Your income level
  - How much you already have in the plan
  - Estimated asset growth rate

They tend to not be worth it until you hit your 30s, but as you get older, it’s not unusual to see a maximum pre-tax retirement contribution of a Cash Balance plan in the hundreds of thousands of dollars!

These plans are notoriously painful and expensive to both set up and administer — but if you are making half a million dollars or more every year, the massive tax deduction more than makes up for it.

And newer providers are continually making it easier to set one up.

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Strategy 4: Have a tax professional calculate the optimal W-2 salary to pay yourself
text:
One of the most important pieces of legislation for US-based business owners came with Trump’s 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA).

Amongst other things, the TCJA gave business owners of passthrough businesses (like LLCs and S-Corps) an automatic tax deduction of up to 20% called the[ Qualified Business Income (QBI) Deduction].

The QBI deduction is a free gift for most business owners, but if you are a high-income earner (roughly ~190Ksingle,~380K married), there are additional restrictions in order to unlock the full deduction.

Specifically, the maximum QBI deduction for high income earners can typically be no more than 50% of the total W-2 wages paid by the business.

What does this mean for you as a high earning S-Corp owner?

You could end up saving more in taxes by paying yourself and your spouse a higher W-2 salary… or at least enough to unlock the full QBI deduction.

I’m not suggesting pulling out the calculator yourself as these calculations do get rather complicated.

But it is absolutely worth finding a tax professional who can run the numbers for you and optimize your W-2 salary.

Getting this number right is alone worth many thousands of dollars every single year.

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Strategy 5: Pay your state taxes from your business
text:
The 2017 TCJA gave most business owners and high tax payers all kinds of tax breaks.

With one big exception.

The TCJA limited the total tax deduction you could claim from paying state and local taxes (SALT) to only $10,000!

This is especially painful for residents of high-tax states like New York or California Imagine making $1M in California, paying $100K+ in state taxes to California and only being able to deduct $10,000 from your federal taxes!

To make matters even worse, the $10,000 limit is the same whether you are single or married filing jointly with two incomes.

This was catastrophic to lots of people in high tax brackets… resulting in most people no longer itemizing deductions (which is needed to claim the SALT deduction) and instead taking the standard deduction.

But the individual states came up with an ingenious workaround for business owners.

Most of them created an “optional tax” that business owners could pay called the[ Pass-Through Entity Tax (PTET)].

This allows you to optionally pay the entirety of your state taxes via your business. This would effectively register the entire payment as a business expense and in effect all your state taxes are now deductible for federal purposes.

Genius, right?

Every state implements the PTET slightly differently so it’s worth reading up on the requirements for your specific state.

But paying this optional tax will end up saving you a lot of money at the highest brackets in high tax states.

You may notice that a lot of these strategies require the help of a tax professional to implement.

It’s imperative you find a CPA that is knowledgable about these strategies since it’s too difficult and painful to DIY most of this.

-----

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Miscellaneous Considerations
text:
I wanted to focus this article on what I consider to be the five most impactful strategies.

But there are a couple of other important things to mention as they can be absolutely vital to get right once your business starts making real money.

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: Expense Tracking and Bookkeeping
text:
At this revenue level, having quality bookkeeping more than pays for itself.

By doing this accurately, you could potentially find more expenses to deduct which would reduce your overall taxable income.

Some opportunities worth looking at here:

1 - Home office deduction

Being a business owner also opens up more tax deductions that W-2 employees don’t have.

If you have a dedicated workspace for the business, you can take the square footage of the workspace, and pro rata deduct it from your rent or mortgage. You could also apply it to furniture, cleaning, utilities etc.

2 - Augusta Rule

If you are not taking the home office deduction, you could look into renting your home to your business for a meeting, offsite, team event etc.

This allows you to pay yourself a fair market rent from your business. And you can legally do this for up to 14 days a year, and owe zero taxes!

3 - Credit card points

If you spend lots of money on ads, OpenAI tokens, building materials or anything really — you can set up a business credit card that gives you a lot of points for those specific expense categories.

You could then use those points to travel in style for you and your family, which works out a potentially very valuable untaxed benefit!

P.S. You may need to deduct the value of the credit card points from your expenses to stay accurate with how the IRS wants to treat this

4 - Prepaying large business expenses

If you are going to have a massively profitable year, you can save money by prepaying software expenses that you would otherwise incur in the next year.

This can be a great way of bringing costs forward, temporarily reducing your profitability, while having larger expenses for the next year prepaid.

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: What the One Big Beautiful Bill Means for High Earners (part 1)
text:
The One Big Beautiful Bill represents nearly $5 trillion in tax changes, with significant benefits for business owners, investors, and high-income earners. This guide breaks down the ten most impactful provisions that could affect your tax planning for years to come.

-----

[On July 4 2025], Trump signed the most significant piece of tax legislation we have had in almost a decade.

Called the “One Big, Beautiful Bill”, this law cements almost $5 trillion in tax cuts… a large majority going to business owners, high-income earners and investors.

While it’s impossible to summarize every single thing in this mammoth piece of legislation, I’m breaking down some of the most significant updates.

Particularly for high-earning professionals, investors and business owners.

-----

1. Lower Tax Rates Made Permanent:

In 2017, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) lowered federal tax brackets for 8 years, as follows:

  - 15% → 12%
  - 25% → 22%
  - 28% → 24%
  - 33% → 32%
  - 39.6% → 37%

We were supposed to revert to the old rates next year, but the new bill makes these reduced rates permanent.

The corporate tax rate on C-Corps remains at a flat 21%, as opposed to a pre-2017 high of 35%.

-----

2. QSBS becomes even more generous:

[QSBS] allows all C-Corp shareholders, typically startup founders, investors and employees to pay no taxes when they sell their shares.

This updated bill makes QSBS even more generous in three separate ways:

1.  Increase of exemption from $10M to $15M

QSBS allowed you to pay no federal taxes (and in most states, also no state taxes) on the maximum of 10 times your basis on the shares or $10 million. This bill updates it to $15 million!

1.  Partial QSBS now kicks in after 3 years

To be eligible for QSBS, you had to hold your shares for 5 years. This new bill introduces partial QSBS as follows:

  - Hold for 3 years - eligible for 50% QSBS deduction
  - Hold for 4 years - eligible for 75% QSBS deduction

1.  A “small business“ can now have up to $75M in assets

QSBS stands for Qualified Small Business Stock. Previously to qualify as a “small business”, the company had to have less than $50M in assets when you acquired your stock.

This bill updates the definition to up to $75M in assets! This means companies that previously may not have been eligible get a second shot at eligibility.

-----

3. 100% Bonus Depreciation is Back:

When you purchase a physical asset like property or machinery, you can typically deduct a small percentage of the purchase price every year as “depreciation”.

Bonus depreciation supercharges this.

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: What the One Big Beautiful Bill Means for High Earners (part 2)
text:
If any asset has a a useful timeline of less than 20 years, bonus depreciation lets you depreciate the entire amount upfront.

This is massively significant for real estate investors!

As a commercial real estate investor, you can pay for a cost segregation study on any property you purchase to break it down into all of its individual components.

You can then take all the components with a quicker depreciation timeline, and use 100% bonus depreciation on those components to get a massive year 1 tax cut.

The upshot is you may be able to get a tax cut of 20%-25% of the purchase price upfront.

If you do go this route, watch out for depreciation recapture if you decide to sell the property at a later point.

-----

4. Relief for software companies as you no longer need to amortize developer salaries over 5 years:

In 2017, the TCJA introduced a massively unpopular measure for software companies stating that they had to amortize developer salaries over 5 years.

This means a business could technically lose money, but still owe taxes as they could only deduct 20% of what they paid a software engineer in the first year.

This caused a lot of chaos in Silicon Valley, and likely was an accelerant for some of the tech layoffs we recently witnessed.

OBBB fixes this, and brings back the ability to full deduct any salaries on R&D and software development in Year 1 for any US-based talent.

Critically, this does not apply for foreign R&D expenses.

-----

5. Permanent increase in the gift and estate tax exemption:

The estate tax exemption used to be $5M for single people, and $10M for married couples prior to the 2017 TCJA.

The TCJA doubled this to $10M single and 20Mmarried,indexedforinflation.Asof2024,theactualnumberswere~14M single and ~$28M married.

However absent of new legislation, this exemption was stated to fall back to the original numbers (adjusted for inflation) at the end of this year.

But OBBB increased it further to $15M single, and $30M for married couples (again, indexed to inflation).

So instead of a halving of the estate tax exemption, we got a further increase and permanently. This is a very meaningful change for the wealthiest households in America.

-----

6. QBI deduction for business owners made permanent:

The 2017 TCJA introduced a new tax deduction of up to 20% for business owners of pass-through businesses like LLCs and S-Corps.

This was called the Qualified Business Income deduction or QBI for short.

This deduction was supposed to sunset in 2026, but the new bill extends this indefinitely!

doc: Ankur's Guide to Save Money on Taxes
title: What the One Big Beautiful Bill Means for High Earners (part 3)
text:
Salary restrictions still apply, and as a high earner, you still need to pay yourself enough in wages to fully maximize this out.

I’ve written more about the QBI deduction in this post on[ The Self-Employed Tax Saving Handbook].

-----

7. Trump accounts for children born between 2025-2029:

All children born between 2025 and 2029 will receive a free $1,000 from the federal government in the new[ Trump Accounts].

These accounts are available to ALL children under the age of 18, even if they aren’t born in those specific years.

These accounts are set to track a major US index like the S&P 500 and parents can contribute an additional post-tax $5,000 a year.

These accounts compound tax-free, and are taxed as long-term capital gains when withdrawn for qualified expenses like education and buying a home.

-----

8. Opportunity zone program made permanent:

I’m a big fan of the[ Qualified Opportunity Zones] tax incentive and have personally benefited from it when I sold my company.

When you have a capital gain, you can immediately roll over the proceeds from the sale into a qualified opportunity zone and defer paying capital gains taxes for 5 years on a rolling basis.

Additionally, if you hold the investment for 10 years, you then also receive an automatic step-up in basis. This effectively means any gains over the last 10 years are completely tax-free!

The opportunity zone program was supposed to sunset, but this legislation extends it indefinitely!

However, new thresholds are being imposed to define exactly what constitutes an opportunity zone moving forward.

-----

9. Legal gambling just became much more expensive:

A big change doing the rounds in the professional gambling communities:

You used to be able to deduct 100% of your gambling losses against your gambling winnings.

However, this bill makes a very significant update allowing gamblers to only deduct up to 90% of their losses against their winnings.

While that may seem like a small change, it is catastrophic for professional gamblers who have a small edge and make money with a high volume of bets.

This now means you could break even gambling… or potentially even lose a small amount of money and still owe significant taxes!

-----

10. State and local tax (SALT) deduction expanded to $40K:

Prior to 2017, taxpayers in high tax states could deduct the entirety of their state and local taxes from their federal tax return if they itemized their taxes.

However, the TCJA limited this SALT deduction to a total of only $10,000 — no matter if you were married or single!

What The Standard Deduction Is

The standard deduction is a fixed amount the government lets everyone subtract from their income before income tax is calculated. You do not have to spend anything or keep any receipts to get it.

It exists so the first slice of what you earn is not taxed at all. Everyone gets it, employees and self-employed people alike, and the amount depends only on your filing status.

|  |  |
| :-: | :-: |
| Single | $16,100 |
| Married filing jointly | $32,200 |
| Head of household | $24,150 |

2026 amounts. They rise most years.

What it does to your bill:

A single person with $50,000 of income does not pay income tax on $50,000. They subtract $16,100 first and pay income tax on what is left.

$50,000 − $16,100 = $33,900 subject to income tax

Someone who earns less than the standard deduction generally owes no income tax at all, because there is nothing left after it comes off.

Two things it does not do:

  - It does not reduce self-employment tax. That tax is calculated separately and the standard deduction never touches it. This is why a self-employed person can owe tax in a year an employee with the same income would owe nothing.
  - It is not the same as your business expenses. Business expenses come off first, to work out your profit. The standard deduction then comes off that profit. You get both.

The alternative almost nobody uses:

Instead of the standard deduction you can add up certain personal expenses — mortgage interest, state taxes, large medical bills, charitable donations — and subtract those instead. That is called itemizing, and you take one or the other, never both.

Roughly 90% of people take the standard deduction, because their itemizable expenses add up to less than the flat amount. Tax software works out which is bigger for you automatically.”

When The IRS May Treat Your Business As A Hobby

You can only deduct business expenses if you are genuinely trying to make money. Work that loses money year after year may be treated as a hobby instead of a business, which sharply limits what you can write off.

This sits underneath everything else in this section. If an activity is not carried on for profit, the deduction rules that apply to businesses do not apply to it.

There is no single test. The IRS weighs a set of factors, including:

  - Whether the activity is carried on in a businesslike way, with proper books
  - The time and effort put in
  - Whether losses are ordinary for a business in its start-up phase
  - Whether methods have been changed in an attempt to improve profitability
  - The taxpayer’s expertise, and any history of making similar activities profitable
  - Whether there are elements of personal pleasure or recreation

A commonly cited guideline is that an activity showing a profit in at least three of the last five years is generally presumed to be for profit. Falling outside that presumption does not settle the question either way — it shifts where the burden sits.

text:

Change:

A Credit Comes Off The Tax; A Deduction Comes Off The Income

A $2,000 deduction saves you $2,000 multiplied by your tax rate — $240 at 12%, $440 at 22%. A $2,000 credit cuts your actual tax bill by the full $2,000, no matter what you earn.

The order in the calculation creates the difference. Deductions are applied before the tax is worked out, so their value depends on the rate. Credits are applied afterwards, straight against the amount owed.

Three kinds, and the difference matters:

  - Nonrefundable — can reduce tax to zero but no further. Anything beyond is lost.
  - Refundable — can go past zero and produce a refund larger than what was paid in.
  - Partially refundable — some of each.

This distinction matters most in low-income years, which are common in self-employment. A nonrefundable credit is worth nothing in a year with no tax liability. A refundable one still pays.

Credits are claimed on the return, and most require a specific form attached. Nearly all have income limits, and most phase out gradually rather than cutting off.

To:

A Credit Comes Off The *Tax*. A Deduction Comes Off The *Income*

A deduction and a credit both sound like $2,000 off, but they aren't.

A deduction comes off your income before tax is calculated. For example, a $2,000 deduction at a tax rate of 12% only saves you $240.

A credit comes off the tax bill itself, after it's been worked out. For example, a $2,000 credit saves you $2,000, at any income level.

Say you owe $5,000 in tax:

|  |  |  |
| :-: | :-: | :-: |
|   | **$2,000 deduction** | **$2,000 credit** |
| Tax bill before | $5,000 | $5,000 |
| What the $2,000 does | Removes $2,000 from your taxable income | Comes straight off the tax bill |
| You save | $240 *(12% of $2,000)* | $2,000 |
| **Tax bill after** | **$4,760** | **$3,000** |

  

Three kinds of tax credits::

A nonrefundable credit stops when your bill hits zero. The leftover $1,500 just disappears and you never see it.

A refundable credit means the government actually pays you if the difference. So your bill hits zero *and* the government pays you the remaining $1,500 in cash.

Partially refundable means part of the credit behaves each way. The Child Tax Credit is $2,200 per child, of which $1,700 is refundable. Therefore, up to $1,700 can come back to you as money, while the other $500 can only cancel out tax you actually owed.

Change:

What Decides The Percentage To Set Aside

How much of each payment you should hold back depends on four things: self-employment tax, which income tax rate your business profit falls into, your state’s tax, and whether a spouse’s job or a second income has already used up the lower tax rates.

There is no single correct figure, because it depends on circumstances a general guide cannot know. The inputs are the same for everyone:

  - Self-employment tax — roughly 15.3% of net profit, calculated on 92.35% of it, with the Social Security portion stopping at $184,500.
  - Federal income tax — which brackets the profit falls into after the standard deduction and the qualified business income deduction.
  - State and local income tax — anywhere from nothing to over 10%.
  - Other household income — a spouse’s salary or a W-2 job fills the lower brackets first, so business profit stacks on top and is taxed at higher rates than it would be alone.

That last input is the one most often overlooked. The same $40,000 of profit produces very different tax depending on what else appears on the return.

Pushing the other way: business expenses reduce both taxes, and adjustments like half of self-employment tax and health insurance premiums come off before income tax is figured. Profit is what gets taxed, not revenue.

Change:

Why Setting Aside Per Payment Beats Saving Up Per Quarter

Putting a set share of every payment into a separate account means the tax payment due every three months is already covered. Waiting until the due date means finding the whole amount from whatever money happens to be left in your account.

The four due dates have nothing to do with when income arrives. Income that comes unevenly — a large project in February, a quiet March, three invoices in April — doesn’t line up with a fixed quarterly demand, and by the due date the money may have gone to a slow month.

Separating as income arrives turns an unpredictable quarterly problem into a predictable per-payment one. Common approaches:

  - A second account that receives a fixed percentage and is used for nothing else
  - An automatic transfer rule, so no decision is required each time
  - Paying the IRS as income arrives — estimated payments can be made any time, not only on the four dates

The account being genuinely separate is what makes the difference. Money in the main account is spendable regardless of what it was mentally labeled.

Taxes When You Have Both A Regular Job And Self-Employment Income

Money you earn on the side sits on top of your wages, so it is taxed at the highest rate your paycheck already pushed you into. Having more tax taken out of that paycheck can cover the tax on your side income, so you may not need quarterly payments at all.

Wages fill the lower brackets first, so business profit is taxed on top of them. This is why side income often produces a larger bill than expected. Self-employment tax still applies to the profit in full, though wages already taxed at the job count toward the $184,500 Social Security cap.

The withholding option:

Withholding from wages is treated as though paid evenly across the year, regardless of when it actually happened. Increasing withholding by filing a new Form W-4 can therefore cover tax on side income without quarterly payments — and can retroactively fix an underpayment from earlier in the year in a way a late estimated payment cannot.

The same applies to a spouse’s job on a joint return.

title: Section 8 (part 4)
text:
At a job, your employer takes tax out of every paycheck and sends it to the IRS for you. That's called withholding. As a self-employed individual, you don't have withholding.

  

However, if you also have a W-2 job, you can take advantage of the withholding option to avoid paying quarterly tax payments on side income.  

  

This is an excellent option to avoid paying interest on payments you’ve failed to make earlier in the year (e.g., the April, June, or September deadline). 

  

Here’s how it works: 

  

1. Four checkpoints, not one finish line.  
 At each deadline, April, June, September, January, the IRS asks: *by this date, had enough been paid?* Not "by the end of the year." By *that* date.

2. Missing a checkpoint starts a clock.  
 If you were $1,500 short in April, a charge starts running on that $1,500 from April onward. It's interest, not a fine. The government was owed money and didn't have it, so they charge for the time they went without. Miss April, June and September and you've got three clocks running.

3. An estimated payment carries the date you sent it.  
 December money is December money. It satisfies the January checkpoint. It cannot travel back and satisfy April, so those three clocks keep running right up until you pay.

4. Withholding is exempt from that, by law.  
 Money withheld from wages is *deemed* to have come out evenly across all four quarters, whatever the actual dates. So $6,000 withheld in December is legally treated as $1,500 sitting there in April, $1,500 in June, and so on. Every checkpoint was met. No clock ever started.

Therefore, increasing withholding by filing a new Form W-4 can retroactively fix an underpayment from earlier in the year in a way a late estimated payment cannot.

How Long To Keep Your Records

Keep your tax records three years in most cases, six years if you left more than 25% of your income off the return, and for as long as you own a piece of property plus three years after you sell it.

Standard period3 years

If income understated by more than 25%6 years

If no return was filedNo limit

Property recordsUntil sold, plus 3 years

The three years run from the filing date or the due date, whichever is later.

Receipts, invoices, bank and card statements, mileage logs and documentation of business purpose all count. Digital copies are acceptable; there is no requirement to keep paper.

For expenses where the business purpose isn’t obvious from the receipt — meals, travel, mixed-use equipment — a note made at the time carries considerably more weight than a reconstruction years later.

Change:

Most IRS Letters Are Not Audits

Most letters from the IRS are computer-generated notices saying a number on your return does not match a form someone sent them, a payment is missing, or the math needs fixing. Each notice has a code in the corner saying exactly what it is about, and a date to reply by.

A common category is a mismatch notice: a form was filed reporting income to the IRS that doesn’t appear on the return. With 1099 thresholds now higher, the reverse situation — income correctly reported with no matching form — is increasingly normal and is not itself a problem.

doc: Tax Guide for Self Employed
title: Section 9 (part 2)
text:
Notices carry a notice number in the corner, which identifies exactly what the letter is and what it asks for. Each has a response deadline, and responding within it generally keeps the matter administrative.

A notice proposing additional tax is a proposal, not a determination. It can be agreed or disputed, and disputing it is a normal process rather than an escalation.

The IRS initiates contact by post. It does not open with a phone call, a text message or an email demanding immediate payment. A first contact arriving by any of those routes is a strong indicator of a scam.

A common category is a mismatch notice. This is when a form was filed reporting income to the IRS that doesn’t appear on the return. With 1099 thresholds now higher, the reverse situation (income correctly reported with no matching form) is increasingly normal and is not itself a problem.

Change:

How To Amend A Return You’ve Already Filed

Form 1040-X is how you correct a return you already sent in. You generally have three years from the day you filed the original return to fix it and claim money back.

Amendments are ordinary. Common reasons include a form arriving after filing, a deduction that was missed, or an error found later.

The refund window is generally three years from the original filing date, or two years from the date the tax was paid, whichever is later. An amendment that increases tax owed does not have that window — it can and generally should be filed as soon as the error is found, since interest accrues in the meantime.

Amended returns take considerably longer to process than original ones. Filing one does not by itself increase audit risk.

doc: PrioritySave video/guide
title: Solo 401(k) basics and 2026 limits (PrioritySave video slides)
text:
A Solo 401(k) is the self-employed version of a 401(k), built for people with no employees (coaches, freelancers, contractors, consultants).
You contribute as both employee and employer. Employee contribution can be pre-tax (deduction now, taxed when withdrawn) or Roth (no deduction now, tax-free when withdrawn). Employer contribution is usually pre-tax only.
Because you contribute twice (employee plus employer), the ceiling is often higher than a W-2 employee's.
Who can open one: anyone with self-employment income and no full-time employees. A spouse is OK, contractors are OK, no LLC needed.
2026 limits: total contribution ceiling $72,000. Employee contribution ceiling $24,500. Employer contribution ceiling is 20% of the business's net profit (or 25% of W-2 wages if operating as an S-corp). The total cannot exceed $72,000. A business must make about $252,000 in profit to reach the full limit with just employee plus employer contributions.
Mega backdoor Roth: a third type of contribution, after-tax, that sits on top of employee and employer contributions to get you to or closer to the $72,000 cap. With it you can reach the cap at about $77,500 of net profit instead of $252,000. Not all Solo 401(k) plans support it. How it works: make normal employee and employer contributions, make an after-tax contribution, then request an in-plan Roth conversion. Convert quickly, because growth earned between contributing and converting is taxed as ordinary income.
Other perks: borrow about half of the balance, up to $50,000, penalty-free. Diverse investments (including real estate and angel investing with the right plan).
Deadlines: existing plan, elect by Dec 31. First-time sole proprietor: up to the filing deadline. S-corp: Dec 31, no exceptions.
Opening one: pick a provider (it does matter which: check whether it allows the mega backdoor Roth and what you can invest in), get an EIN, sign the documents, fund it.

doc: PrioritySave video/guide
title: S-corp vs sole proprietor vs LLC (PrioritySave video script)
text:
A sole proprietorship is the default if you do nothing. Profit flows to your personal return on Schedule C and all of it is subject to self-employment tax.
An LLC is a legal structure, not a tax structure. It gives liability protection, but by default the IRS taxes a single-member LLC exactly like a sole proprietorship, so forming one does not change your tax bill.
An S-corp is not a business structure, it is a tax election filed by an LLC or corporation. It splits income into a salary and a profit distribution, and self-employment tax only applies to the salary portion.
Example: $150,000 profit, $90,000 salary. Employment tax drops from about $21,200 as a sole proprietor to about $13,800 as an S-corp, a $7,400 savings. But the 20% business deduction shrinks because salary is not business profit, adding about $4,100 of income tax. Net savings are closer to $3,300, not $7,400.
The commonly cited $75,000 to $100,000 breakeven ignores that lost deduction. Running an S-corp costs about $1,400 to $3,200 a year (payroll service plus Form 1120-S). Across $60,000 to $200,000 of profit, real net savings are only about $2,300 to $4,000 before running costs, sometimes barely positive or negative at the low end. Some states and cities (New York City is the classic example) tax S-corps in ways that can wipe out the savings.
At high income the bigger reason to elect S-corp is the 20% deduction. Above $201,750 (single) or $403,500 (married filing jointly) the deduction is limited by W-2 wages. A sole proprietor pays $0 in W-2 wages so the deduction can disappear. Example at $400,000 profit: sole prop gets none of the 20% deduction, an S-corp paying $240,000 salary keeps a $29,016 deduction, a $13,252 difference mostly unrelated to employment tax.
Limits: salary must be reasonable (too low risks reclassification as wages plus back taxes, interest and penalties). Retirement contributions can shrink because the employer contribution is based on W-2 wages. Reversing an election generally means waiting 5 years to elect again.
To elect: form or have an LLC or corporation, file Form 2553, set up payroll and pay a reasonable salary, keep business and personal finances separate. Form 2553 is due within 2 months and 15 days after the start of the tax year you want it to apply to, or any time in the preceding year.

doc: PrioritySave video/guide
title: Entity guide: LLC liability, S-corp costs, 2026 wage base, BOI (PrioritySave guide)
text:
Costs: sole proprietor costs nothing. LLC costs about $35 to $500 to set up and $0 to $800 a year depending on state (California highest at $800). An S-corp adds roughly $700 to $3,500 a year for payroll and the company tax return.
An LLC does not protect against your own professional negligence, debts you personally guarantee, unpaid payroll taxes, fraud, or claims where you did not keep personal and business finances separate. For most solo self-employed people, professional liability insurance and good contract terms (limitation of liability, clear scope) do more practical protection than an entity.
S-corp components to weigh: payroll tax saved (about 15.3% of income taken as distribution instead of salary), added admin cost (about $1,500 to $4,000 a year), QBI deduction lost (20% of income moved from distribution to salary), and the Social Security wage base. For 2026 the 12.4% Social Security portion applies only to the first $184,500; above that only 2.9% Medicare continues, plus 0.9% additional Medicare tax above $200,000 single or $250,000 married filing jointly.
Reasonable compensation has no published formula. IRS factors include training and experience, duties, time devoted, what you would pay someone else, and industry norms.
S-corp eligibility: no more than 100 shareholders, no non-resident alien shareholders, one class of stock.
BOI reporting: as of August 2026 FinCEN's final rule removed the beneficial ownership reporting requirement for US companies and US persons. Foreign entities registered in the US still report. Some states have their own versions. Be skeptical of services charging BOI filing fees.
Sources for 2026 figures: IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32, IRS Notice 2025-67, SSA contribution and benefit base.
